subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FREIGHT ASSISTANCE ON MOVEMENT OF SEED OATS

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Acting Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FREIGHT ASSISTANCE ON MOVEMENT OF SEED OATS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of last summer's drought in western Canada, many areas in Manitoba and Saskatchewan are without adequate supplies of seed oats. The governments of these two provinces have requested the dominion government to share with them on a fifty-fifty basis the cost of a program of freight assistance to move seed oats into deficit areas. The cabinet has authorized federal participation in a program of this kind.
The assistance provided will be limited to a maximum of 75 per cent of the total freight costs and also to a maximum of $12 per ton. Assistance will be paid only if the distance the oats are to be moved is greater than 25 miles.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the prairie farmers who are involved will welcome this announcement, but the members of this group do hope this is not in any way related to a coming election.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, March 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Churchill for the second reading of Bill No. C-75, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, CONTROL OF DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate adjourned last night I had been pointing out that the extension of the Canadian Wheat Board Act was something that would receive the overwhelming support of the producers in western Canada, and that over the years the Canadian wheat board had served the interests of the grain producers in a very efficient manner.
I had also referred to the discussions that had taken place to bring about another international wheat agreement, and the Minister of Veterans Affairs correctly pointed out two main reasons why the surplus grain situation no longer exists. The first of these, and I think this is the minor one, is the increase in Canadian sales of wheat, and the second reason is the very widespread drought experienced last year which followed a number of years of less than average rainfall. The minister also pointed out that 99 per cent of the delivery points are now on an open quota; but I contend that the grain producers, from the standpoint of potential income within the next few months, are in a very serious situation.
The anticipated deliverable grain from March 1, 1962 to July 31, 1962 totals 177.2 million bushels. This includes all grains, and I would point out that the figure for the same period last year was 554 million bushels. Therefore the income position of grain producers will be very serious during the next few months. This is not the occasion to advocate legislation to bolster farm income, particularly in relation to potential crop failures, but the government should take action in other legislation to protect the farmers from what is a very serious financial crisis at this time.
We have heard many statements about when the election will take place. I have guessed before and guessed wrongly. I probably could guess wrongly again, but the Prime Minister announced that the final payments, after all possible expenditures have been flushed out of the wheat board funds, will be in the producers' hands by May 28. I think that at least has some significant bearing on the date, of the election. I am not complaining in any way about the action that has been taken to make interim payments, or about the government doing everything possible to put more money in the pockets of the grain producers at the present time.
26207-1-141
but one can only wonder whether this action would be taken in a non-election year, or whether this is an instance of government action being influenced by the proximity of the general election.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs used some statistics to show the improvement being brought about in the ceiling prices by reason of the change in the international wheat agreement. It has been said that there can be a 12.5 cents increase per bushel in the prices to producers because of the increase in the ceiling, but I would like the minister to explain why the present selling price for No. 1 Northern wheat out of Fort William and Port Arthur is $1.90 plus a fraction of a cent, which is about nine cents lower than the maximum under the present international wheat agreement in terms of the Canadian dollar. Our dollar is at a discount today, and the maximum price for wheat under the international wheat agreement is certainly not being obtained for the grain that is being sold out of Fort William/Port Arthur. How can the minister contend, when the wheat board is unable to get the maximum price for wheat under the agreement at this time, that there is any real possibility of getting the maximum in discounted Canadian dollars, to which the minister referred last night, of $2.14 a bushel? I think the minister is just fooling the farmers when he puts forward those figures as a realistic possibility. I suggest to him that they are not; that as the minister introducing this legislation he probably knows they are not, and that he should not be using statistics of this kind.
My main question is this. Why is the wheat board unable to get the maximum price today for wheat out of Fort William/Port Arthur? And if it cannot get it now, why does the minister imply that the wheat board may be able to get the maximum price under the new wheat agreement which will come into effect on August 1?
This amendment gives us an opportunity to review the operation of the wheat board over a five year period, as the minister has said. There has been established under the wheat board something which is called a special account. The money in this fund was accumulated as a result of the fact that certain sums credited to grain producers from time to time have not been claimed. This money is set aside in what is called a special account, and it can be used upon the authority of an order in council set up by the government in what the government believes to be, or says it believes to be, in the interests of the grain producers. In the crop year 1959-60 an order in council was passed which is referred to in this report

Canadian Wheat Board Act as PC/1960/519. This took $775,000 of the farmers' money out of this special account to pay to the United Grain Growers Limited because they had an accident in one of their terminals at Port Arthur. The report states:
On September 23, 1959, the out-shore annex of the United Grain Growers Limited terminal elevator "A" at Port Arthur, Ontario, collapsed. The collapse resulted in the loss of 1,914,760.1 bushels of wheat, oats and barley valued at $2,406,175.22.
This was a loss suffered by one elevator company. True, it was a farmers' elevator company, but I suggest it is not a proper use of this fund to take $775,000 out of this special account and pay it to a single elevator company. The moneys in this account should be used, in my judgment, for the general advantage of all grain producers, and not as a kind of slush fund out of which dollars are made available to an elevator company because it lost certain sums as the result of an accident. I think such an accident as this is an ordinary risk which the company itself should cover by putting away proper reserves for an emergency, taking out insurance and so on. I would ask the minister when he speaks to tell us why it seemed appropriate to take this $775,000 out of the special account and pay it to one elevator company which had suffered a certain loss in grain in a terminal elevator.
The minister wound up his statement last evening by saying that the Canadian government, in presenting this bill, had demonstrated its support of the wheat board as a marketing agency for wheat, oats and barley. However, during the term of office of this government the jurisdiction and the effectiveness of the Canadian wheat board have been undermined. They have been undermined in relation to the sale of feed grain to the feed mills in the prairie provinces. The first excuse was that the wheat board did not have the legal jurisdiction to ensure its quota regulation. Then certain references were made to the supreme court, and the jurisdiction of the wheat board was upheld. But even in the face of this decision by the supreme court, members on the government side of this house carried on an attack directed against the wheat board, an attack on the marketing of oats and barley on the prairies by the wheat board to the feed mills. Led by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) and in face of stated opposition from the wheat board and from all the farm organizations, except perhaps one, they were able to remove the jurisdiction of the wheat board in this field.

The hon. member for Melville, who is a genial member, believes that the jurisdiction of the wheat board should be tested even further in the courts. He believes that in future the wheat board should have to go to the Minister of Agriculture to get permission to prosecute wrongdoers who have been bootlegging grain from the prairie provinces across interprovincial boundaries.
I suggest that if this course were to be followed the whole system of the orderly marketing of grain in Canada would be completely undermined. I think the system of orderly marketing built up over the years under the wheat board system has been a good one. I think it should be protected, and

I think the policy of the government with regard to feed mills has been a mistake.
The Minister of Agriculture said that before the end of the crop year, July 31, 1961, he would provide for further submissions before he made his policy for the present year clear and final. My understanding from the farm organizations is that he has never consulted them. He never gave them a chance to make representations. He merely went forward in the present crop year with this policy which has undermined the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board. I think any reference to the courts in the future instituted or supported by members of parliament or the government to restrict the areas of jurisdiction would be a great mistake. The Canadian wheat board is today supported by farm organizations and producers. Instead of attempting to tear down the jurisdiction of the wheat board as it now exists I feel further steps should be taken to strengthen the wheat board, to restore the jurisdiction it once had and to make it a more effective organization in the marketing of producers' grain both within Canada and in export trade.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should simply like to add a few remarks to those of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) on the Canadian wheat board.
On March 26, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) replied to a question put by my colleague from Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger). The third part of starred question No. 315 reads as follows:
How many vacancies have occurred since 1957?
And here is the answer, as found on page 2157 of Hansard for March 26, 1962:
The Canadian Wheat Board Act provides for the appointment by the governor in council of

not less than three nor more than five commissioners. At no time have there been five commissioners serving on the board. Since 1957 there have been two resignations and two appointments.
The fourth part of the question asked by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska reads as follows:
Give the name, address and qualification of those appointed to fill such vacancies?
And here is the reply given by the minister:
4. Mr. J. T. Dallas was appointed a commissioner on September 1, 1958 and resigned on December 31, 1960, Mr. J. B. Lawrie was appointed a commissioner December 22, 1961. Prior to their appointments Mr. Dallas was executive vice president of the Continental Grain Company, Winnipeg, Manitoba, and Mr. Lawrie was European manager of the Canadian wheat board, London, England. Both these gentlemen, because of their successful association over many years with the Canadian grain trade in executive capacities, were highly qualified to assume the responsibilities of commissioners of the Canadian wheat board.
I remember very well, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Agriculture-following several requests made by eastern farmers and representations by my colleague from Drummond-Arthabaska, as well as by a few others of my colleagues-while he may not have promised it, certainly gave us to understand that he would appoint to the board a representative from the eastern provinces who would see that the interests of the eastern farmers, that is the farmers in Ontario, Quebec, the maritime provinces and Newfoundland, are protected.
I suggest that the minister should have had the time to make the appointment since that statement was made.
Before my hon. colleague from St. Hya-cinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) gets up and charges me of trying to set the western farmers against the eastern farmers, I should like to add that we are very glad indeed to note that the hon. members from the west are looking after their constituents, the western farmers. Such is their duty and they do not fail in that duty.
But, without wanting to set the western farmers against the eastern farmers, it is also our duty to look particularly after the farmers in Ontario, Quebec, the maritime provinces and Newfoundland. That cannot be challenged. For once, I should like the Minister of Agriculture to look into this problem and to help us to refute certain ideas currently expressed throughout the province; he should see that everyone is given a fair deal, for the people of Quebec-as well as those of Ontario-are Canadian citizens just like the people of the western provinces.
We are all proud to belong to the same country, Canada, but we wish to see every-
Canadian Wheat Board Act body treated on an equal footing, in the ten provinces. That is what we are asking.
I should also like to ask the Minister of Agriculture, or the hon. gentleman who is representing him in the house, if he intends to allow eastern farmers to buy directly from western farmers, without having to go through brokers, wholesalers or the Canadian wheat board. Since such a privilege is granted to western farmers, I wonder why the Minister of Agriculture should not give a similar one to eastern farmers.
One of the parliamentary secretaries to the minister said a while ago that they first have to know public opinion before they can make changes in the regulations of the Canadian wheat board. Hearing such an argument makes me wonder.
The hon. member for Assiniboia stated in very plain language that there was discrimination in that field. The government knows about that. Why should they have to wait for public opinion to take action? Do their actions depend on public opinion? Do they give more consideration to the votes they can get from public opinion than to justice towards all Canadian citizens?
That is the question I put to him and I should like to have an answer. Especially, I should like to hear someone tell me if, before long, eastern Canada will be represented on the Canadian wheat board.

Canadian Wheat Board Act by the hon. member for Lapointe. After listening to his speech and that of the hon. member for Assiniboia I found that they took opposite sides of the fence, and I wondered which one was the true Liberal after all. The hon. member has had his chance to make his speech. If he will just give me a few moments in which to do so, I will deal with the history of the Canadian wheat board.
If you go back, Mr. Speaker, to June 13, 1935, volume IV of the debates of the House of Commons, or in fact if you go through the whole volume you will see that it is made up of the debate on the Canadian wheat board. I think it is time some western Conservative member set the record straight once and for all, and made it clear that the Canadian wheat board came about through the instrumentality of a great Conservative who represented a part of my riding of Bow River but which at that time was called Calgary West. I refer to none other than the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. The farmers of Alberta, and I am sure the farmers of Saskatchewan, know that it was R. B. Bennett who created the Canadian wheat board as a result of which there was, in the words of the hon. member for Assiniboia, some facsimile of organized marketing.
One cannot deal with these amendments without going briefly into the history of the wheat board. Just read the debates. Who was it who talked for days and months in 1935, delaying the legislation creating the Canadian wheat board? None other than the Liberal party. That may be why the Liberal party had to go elsewhere for a representative from the Canadian west at this time. It is the reason they have had no representation in western Canada.
The farmers know who their friends are. The farmers know who created the wheat board and who are the friends of the wheat board. There has been talk about undermining the wheat board, but who was it who opposed R. B. Bennett in 1935 when he tried to create the board? The Liberal party; they opposed it. When the bill was brought in at that time they talked for days on the Canada Grain Act, out of which gradually grew the Canadian wheat board as we know it today. There is not a Liberal here who will stand up in his place this afternoon and deny that the foundation for the creation of the Canadian wheat board was the Conservative party. In fact, to the farmers of western Canada the Canadian wheat board is Mr. Conservative.
It is all hogwash for the Liberals to talk about undermining the wheat board and for them to say that the hon. member for Hum-boldt-Melfort-Tisdale who sits in front of me, has suggested that the Conservatives have

not been playing ball with the Canadian wheat board. I should like to say here that it is because of the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale, whose riding I know well because I lived there for almost 10 years, that rapeseed is now classified as a grain. As a member from another province I wish to congratulate the hon. member, because this shows what one Conservative is doing and it shows that we all work together for the common good of the western farmers.
Another charge was made in connection with the new international wheat agreement. It is not so many years ago that the western farmer when he was leaning over his back fence and talking to you would say, "Why did C. D. Howe not compromise to the extent of five cents a bushel", so that an international wheat agreement could have been consummated by those countries that wished to buy the best wheat in the world from western Canada? It was the Liberals who made the mistake, and it is time it was put on the record that because of that mistake a surplus of some 700 million bushels of wheat was piled up in bins, on the ground, in barns and other buildings, all stored in western Canada when we took office. However, because of the dynamic action of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton, Qu'Appelle) we were able to unload the surplus created by the former administration. The western farmer knows what I say is correct, because wherever you go western farmers will tell you exactly what I am saying in this chamber today.
The hon. member speaks about the Saskatchewan wheat pool. Everybody in Saskatchewan and Alberta knows that it was a Conservative government that kept the wheat pools in operation financially during the depression of the 30's. They know who are the friends of the wheat pools, the friends of the co-operatives and the farmers. Let us see what some of these distinguished men have had to say about the international wheat agreement. I refer now to the Wheat Pool Budget of March 16, 1962, where I find the following:
In view of greatly reduced supplies in most wheat exporting countries, exporters had hoped to get a somewhat higher ceiling.
It is obvious that the farmers want more for their wheat and everything they sell, but at the same time they are fair. We all want the best price.
G. L. Harrold, president of the Alberta wheat pool who attended the Geneva meeting, said: "We had hoped for another 2J cents", and that the current increase is "probably a compromise".
Let us pause there for a moment, Mr. Speaker. Was it not better that we reach a

compromise than turn down the agreement, as C. D. Howe did under the former administration, thus letting surplus wheat pile up on the prairies so the farmers could not meet their obligations? Let us see what the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool had to say about the recent agreement. These are men who represent farm organizations and speak for the farmers, and when the hon. member for Assiniboia says that we are undermining the wheat board or undermining the farm organizations the farmers just do not agree with him.

Canadian Wheat Board Act of Trade and Commerce the government, through the Minister of Agriculture and the former minister of agriculture, has been able to negotiate large sales of wheat to communist China and other countries and unload the surplus. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. Maybe the change should have been made in the days of C. D. Howe, because I am confident that Mr. Gardiner would have liked to have the wheat board under his thumb. He could not get along very well with Mr. Howe. When we hear loose criticism of that nature I wonder whether the Liberals are not looking for something to talk about in the hope of influencing somebody and confusing the people enough so the odd farmer may vote for them. It will take more than the hon. member for Assiniboia, the new member of the Liberal party, to convince the farmers of western Canada that they need the Liberal party to look after their interests.
Let us review the situation. The Conservative party has always stood solidly behind the wheat board. We created it, and we believe it is a good marketing institution. It organized the sellers so they could deal with the organized buyers. We also believe that the Canadian wheat board should be under the Department of Agriculture, because then you have the proper relationship between the Minister of Agriculture and the board, and the minister can work hand in hand with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his department. However, in all the time I was clerk of the privy council, which after all was only one year, and in all the time I was a bureaucrat, which was rather longer than that, and all the time I have been a member of this house, I have never read an order in council quite like this one. I should like to think, sir, I was eloquent enough to describe this order in council in the way it would have been described by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) if he had been on this side of the house and this order in council had been passed by the previous government.
This is the order in council which guarantees this China wheat sale. The government were scared to come to the house and ask parliament to vote a guarantee as they should have done. They preferred, in a backhanded fashion, to give a guarantee, and let us look at the legal authority for it. I quote: His Excellency
The Governor General in Council:
His excellency the governor general in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance-
[Mr. Pickersgill.)
This is not done on the recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce or any of these other lesser lights, but upon the recommendation of that super guardian of the treasury, 18 hours a day, the Minister of Finance.
-pursuant to the Canadian Wheat Board Act-

-is pleased hereby to authorize the Minister of Finance (a) to give to the Canadian wheat board an undertaking-
Just listen to this, sir.

Well, talk about contempt of parliament; talk about taking parliament for granted; talk about an arrogant attitude, this is an assumption by hon. gentlemen opposite that they will always occupy the treasury benches, because this is a long term arrangement. What is the undertaking? It is that they will come to parliament and ask for this money; that is the kind of guarantee that they purport to give. It is no wonder it was so difficult to get any of these details out of the government.

This is the kind of undertaking given to the wheat board, which the wheat board was no doubt obliged to accept and keep quiet about. speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-28 to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1960, with respect to representation in the Senate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Before calling on the hon. member who moves the bill, may I remind the house that the last time this bill was called I raised the question as to whether it might be a money bill requiring a resolution and the authority of the ministry before it could be proceeded with. I have come to the conclusion, subject to such persuasion as may be exercised by hon. members who wish to discuss the point, that it is not clearly enough a money bill for me to take the responsibility of preventing debate. I am therefore disposed to allow the mover to proceed, unless some hon. member wishes to object to that course and persuades me it is not the right course.
I think I should state briefly what considerations arise, because it is not without importance. Bill No. C-28 provides for an amendment to sections 21 and 22 of the British North America Act so as to increase the number of senators from 102, the present number, to 104. In other words, the bill provides for the addition of two senators to the Senate. Now the consequence of passing this bill would be that those senators, under the provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act, chapter 249 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, would become entitled to compensation as senators and would be paid accordingly. So an indirect consequence of passing this bill would be to expend from the public purse the emoluments which are payable under another act to the two additional senators, after they have been appointed. The consequence of passing the bill would, therefore, be an expenditure of public funds.
However, I rather take the view that the expenditure of public funds is already


authorized by the Senate and House of Commons Act which provides for the payment of senators apparently in anticipation of the appointment of additional senators as well as of additional members of parliament. So authority for payment has already been given by parliament. It was given when it passed the Senate and House of Commons Act; and this bill, which does not in itself provide for any payment, might therefore be regarded as not being a money bill, even though it sets in motion the other act and would, therefore, involve expenditure.
There is one precedent, and it is on the basis of this precedent that I propose to allow the matter to proceed. There is the Representation Act, chapter 15 of the statutes of 1952 called an Act to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1951, with respect to the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons. This was introduced as Bill No. 221 on June 10, 1952. It was introduced without notice. It was not preceded by resolution, nor did it have the recommendation of the crown, although as a result of the bill the number of members of the House of Commons was increased from 255 to 265 and an additional member was provided for the Northwest Territories. In that case the house proceeded to increase the number of members of parliament and thereby to increase the emoluments to which members were entitled. It seems the cases are parallel. It is the only precedent and, therefore, I think the proper course would be to register this query about the bill so that it will not stand in the way of future decisions, but not to press the point to the extent that debate would be discontinued.
I am reinforced in my view by thinking that one should settle these matters giving the benefit of the doubt to the authority of a private member of the house to proceed to raise such matters as he thinks may properly be brought before parliament, not by ruling in a restrictive way.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I hope the house will be as disposed to the acceptance of this bill as it was to the acceptance of the measure which I introduced a short while ago in connection with representation for the Keewatin and Franklin districts. The same reasons are applicable in support of representation in the other place for these areas of northern Canada,

perhaps to an even greater extent because we are dealing here with all that land mass and all those Arctic islands north of the 60th parallel, whose residents at the moment have no specific representation in the other place.
With the passage of the bill dealing with the extension of the franchise, or, rather, the facilities enabling Canadian citizens living in the Keewatin and Franklin districts to cast their ballots, no other Canadians remain in our nation who do not now have the opportunity to cast their votes and, by so doing, take part in the government of Canada. I gave as supporting reasons in favour of that bill that the citizens of Canada should not be taxed without having the opportunity of being heard in the parliament of Canada. I think it is trite to say that the parliament of Canada consists of two houses, this House of Commons as well as the other place. Matters concerning taxation are discussed here and laws concerning the taxation of Canadians are made in this chamber; but before their final passage they are considered, accepted, rejected or amended by the members of the other place. Surely, then, the Canadians of the north should be entitled to be heard on these matters in the other place.
It seems to me it is important to recognize the fundamental right that in a free and democratic society such as ours in Canada every adult Canadian is by law clothed with the right to take part in government. I advanced this argument in discussing the amendment to the Representation Act which I brought before the house a few weeks ago and I advance it again. The people of Canada in all parts of the country have a right to take part in their government and in my view the government of Canada consists of both houses of parliament.
This principle was embodied in the four kinds of rights to which I drew the attention of the house when I last spoke on my bill to amend the Representation Act, the rights expressed in the principles to which the United Nations dedicated itself in the universal declaration of human rights in 1948, a declaration which grew out of the public demand for recognition of the advancement of equal rights among all members of the human family.
In support of my argument that all Canadians have the right to be represented in both houses of parliament I would draw the attention of the house to the British North America Act of 1886 which is to be found in the Revised Statutes of Canada, volume 6, at page 159 where, after the preamble, it is set forth in section 1 that:
The parliament of Canada may from time to time make provision for the representation In the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, or in either of them, of any territories which for
British North America Act the time being form part of the dominion of Canada, but are not included in any province thereof.
In section 2 of the same act it is set forth that:
Any act passed by the parliament of Canada before the passing of this act for the purpose mentioned in this act shall, if not disallowed by the Queen, be, and shall be deemed to have been, valid and effectual from the date at which it received the assent, in Her Majesty's name, of the Governor General of Canada.
The act goes on to discuss the making of provisions for adding to the membership of the House of Commons and the other place. In effect, the act gives us the right to amend our own constitution as found in the British North America Act in so far as such an amendment may effect an addition to the House of Commons or to the Senate.
The second point I made in discussing my argument in support of extending the facilities of the franchise to the residents of the Keewatin and Franklin districts of the Northwest Territories was in relation to the Canadian Bill of Rights. I think it is of paramount importance, and I am sure all hon. members of the house will agree with me, that the Canadian Bill of Rights affords its protection to all Canadians regardless of their race, colour, creed or religion, and that essential protection is that there shall be no discrimination as between Canadians. It seems we fall short of the principle expressed in the Canadian Bill of Rights if we continue to refuse to grant to northern Canadians above the sixtieth parallel the right to have a voice in the other half of the Canadian parliament.
There are other and valid reasons for the house giving favourable consideration to this measure. I realize that the bill comes before us at a rather awkward time since there is a resolution on the order paper calling for the setting up of an independent commission to inquire into the redistribution of seats in this house. It might be one of the terms of reference of that commission that they may be called upon to look into the desirability of redistribution in the other place as well; of this I am not aware.
Another argument I would advance in support of the house adopting this measure is the developing autonomy of both the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. I wish to deal with those two territories for a brief moment.
In the Yukon territory we have a long history of the development of autonomy and we are rapidly approaching the point where we can see in the near future the possibility that the Yukon might become Canada's eleventh province. Certainly there is every reason for anticipating this development. It would seem incongruous in the light

British North America Act of the development there and the increasing population and industry that we should continue to turn a blind eye to the fact that the area is without representation in the Senate. The Yukon has had a sitting member in the House of Commons since 1902 after the Yukon was created a separate district, having been carved out of the Northwest Territories in 1901. In the Northwest Territories, the Mackenzie district has had a sitting member since the amendment of the Representation Act in 1947. As hon. members will recall the first sitting member for that district came to this house in 1949. We are slowly progressing toward the development of the political autonomy of the north and it seems to me the next logical step that should be taken by this House of Commons and by the Senate is to provide a voice for the people of the north in the other place.
Canada above the sixtieth parallel constitutes 40 per cent of the nation. I do not think the argument rests on the number of people in that area. It is a particular area, an Arctic area, and it has special problems. Those problems have to be voiced in as wide a fashion as possible in both places. I think it is not unreasonable to suggest that since the appointment has been made to the other place of a member of the Indian race we might anticipate the appointment to the Senate of an Eskimo to voice the views of those people who number approximately 10,000 in the Canadian north.
There may be those who say that in the development of this trend toward the greater autonomy of the north the federal government largely subsidizes the areas, and therefore we as the House of Commons should continue administering those areas until such time as the population and industry of the Canadian north reach the stage where autonomy is economically justifiable. I would simply refer those hon. members who take that view to the province of Manitoba in the years immediately before it became a province, when the local territorial government was heavily subsidized by the federal government and yet the province achieved autonomy while in the position of being so subsidized.
Of course there is the classic current example of Newfoundland, which is now heavily subsidized by federal funds. I think I should not leave the presentation of this bill without also remarking on the recent resolution passed by the Northwest Territories council when they met here last January. It suggested that from the existing three administrative divisions in the Northwest Territories we should carve out two new Canadian areas. The present area of the Northwest Territories is one third of the whole of Canada, to put

the matter in another form. On the northeast it snuggles right against Greenland and on the west it is flanked by the Yukon. At one point it is a mere 100 miles from Alaska. It is true that there are only 23,000 people in this vast expanse of the Northwest Territories. However, the council, when it met here last spring, began dividing the territories into two pieces. That was a logical move, in my view, and one which I think lays the groundwork for suggesting to this house in the near future that, once the division is made, it might be the time for introducing a measure which would give both the western and the eastern portion of the Northwest Territories a member in this house.
There are other arguments that can be advanced in support of the measure before the house. When one agrees to the principle that Canadians have a right to be represented in the Canadian parliament, I feel that the house would be remiss if it did not accept the principle that it does not restrict the representation spoken of to a right to be heard in the House of Commons. I contend that this right embraces also the right to be heard in the other place, where every piece of legislation passed by this house must be considered. Certainly the voice of the north cannot be heard in its entirety if, with respect to the opinions and views of the Canadian people who live in the north and who are pioneering the area above the sixtieth parallel, we restrict that right to one chamber, namely this House of Commons.
I believe there are others who wish to speak on the principle of the bill, Mr. Speaker. With the simple urging to the members of the house to lend support to this measure I will now take my seat in order that those others might be heard.

have been bringing forward with such emphasis and such force that they have been able to commend themselves to the government and in due course have received the approval of the government and have become part of the law of this country.
I do not wish to traverse many of the points which have been dealt with over the past several years in connection with the north, its needs and requirements. I have a sympathetic feeling toward the principle involved in this bill. I represent a constituency which in size is more than a third of that of the province of Alberta. I know what it is like to be obliged to travel substantial distances. I know what it is like to be obliged to meet with a variety of problems of a number of people scattered over a great distance. That is one of the problems which beset the Yukon and the Northwest Territories at this particular time.
I know that the hon. member for Yukon is a member of the same profession as that to which I have the honour to belong. I know what is involved for him in representing at this particular time, when it is in the midst of its growing pains this tremendous area of the Yukon which will in due course, I believe, evolve into a greater, far more populous and much more economically prosperous region.
I can enumerate many of these problems and I do so because I think they have a bearing on the particular issue which the hon. member has raised. The hon. member referred to his hope that if this bill should in due course be approved and become part of our law and if a new senator was to be appointed, such senator might be a person of the Eskimo race. I heartily approve and second that proposition. I know many of the Eskimo people. I have travelled a good deal in the north. The Eskimos are fine people. They are now at a difficult period in their development from a simple nomadic race. Coming in contact in recent years with white people, white settlements and white industrial development they have discovered the problems which under those circumstances they are bound to experience. I think it would be a splendid idea to see in the other place a member of the Eskimo race, someone to speak for them, to tell of their problems and of the difficulties which they have experienced in the past and are bound to experience over the new generation. I think of the Indians. While we have, of course, legislation to some extent dealing with them, those who live in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon have particular and special problems of their own over and above the difficulties of the Indians in the other parts of Canada. I think of the economic changes which are now approaching in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon. I say all these
British North America Act things, Mr. Speaker, because I think they bear strictly on the problem for which I believe this bill will provide the cure.
I stop here to emphasize that there should be that additional representation in the parliament of Canada to which that particular part of our country is entitled. I know that the hon. member for Yukon has a great task to perform and he is performing it ably and adequately. I was well acquainted with the late member for Mackenzie River. I visited Yellowknife and district for several days last summer and had the privilege of meeting him and talking to him there on his return from an extended trip which he had made with his family into the vast hinterland of his constituency, an exhausting and demanding task even for one in the best of health. As I listened to the hon. member for Yukon speak it struck me that there should be additional assistance in the form of senatorial representation at this time to deal with all the problems that arise.
Great things are about to happen in the north country and I say that generally, not wishing to precipitate any particular issue at this time. Within the existing limits of the British North America Act and our own laws we have done certain things. We have provided a judiciary for the Yukon and Northwest Territories. We have provided the incipient beginnings of representative government by means of a territorial council both in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon. But we must look ahead to the time, in the not too distant future, when there may be additional political units in the form of provinces to add to the 10 we already have in Canada. This matter has been referred to by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources from time to time, as well as by other members of the house. I know that at the present time the population is not large but I believe I am correct when I call the attention of hon. members to the fact that as a result of the last census it now appears that the rate of population growth has been greater in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon than in any other part of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext: It is 60.8 per cent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Yukon for drawing to my attention the fact that it is 60.8 per cent. When I am home in the summer, in my riding of Peace River, the pathway to the north, day by day I see tremendous numbers of cars with tourists going north as well as others with people going in there with the intention of carving out for themselves a new home and a new career. This is one of the few places left on this continent where it is possible for men of courage, industry and imagination to go

British North America Act and, without too much influence or too much money, be able to establish a home for their families and a business and career for themselves.
From what I know, Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied that the fantastically high rate of increase in population is bound to continue. It is inevitable; it cannot be stayed. I believe it is up to us at this time to make a complete survey of the whole situation so that when new provinces are created, when larger populations become a fact, when new industries are established and we see a quickening of the economic pulse of the north we will have provided the necessary machinery of government so that the people there will have complete and adequate representation.
Someone has described the other place, I believe, as the repository of sober second thought. If that is the case, I am quite sure that any representation from the north will be largely influential in providing some change in that spirit. We heard something about that the other day in a debate, if I may be permitted to refer to it, when we talked about certain improvements to the old town of Dawson city. I would think that the spirit of Robert Service might well flourish in the other place.
On another aspect of the matter, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that it often happens, as was the case last year, that there are differences of opinion between the two bodies. This, of course, is the right of both. It might well be that the people of the Northwest Territories should be entitled to have representation in the other place so that they might be free to take a different view from that which we happen to take in this house.
I want to be careful in phrasing my final point. I know many people who went into the north country who have expressed the view I wish to express, and I have been there myself and have experienced this attitude of the people. Up until recent years the people there felt that Ottawa was a long distance away and that there was a complete lack of understanding, sympathy and appreciation of the point of view of the northerner, which I may say is completely different from that found elsewhere in this country. I do not wish to be critical in any sense of the departmental officials who went to that part of the country because in many ways they were faced with difficult tasks when they left other parts of Canada to make their homes in the north. They had difficulty in understanding, assimilating and interpreting the views of the people there. However, the people there felt that on too many occasions there was a lack of understanding on the

part of certain officials of what were the real requirements not only of the present but of the future.
Therefore, it is my view that if this bill as proposed ultimately becomes law it will have the effect of interposing additional representation in the form of two senators, one from each of these geographical units, so that the true views and real desires of the people in these territories can be presented personally in Ottawa by people who have lived in the territories and who have experienced the problems of the people of the north. For all these reasons I am most happy to lend my voice and support to what has been said by the hon. member for Yukon, and I hope the time may not be too far distant when we may look forward to the arrival in Ottawa of senators from the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
It is
obvious, Mr. Speaker, as will be proven by the time the clock reaches six, that the government does not support this measure. However, I should like to say a few words upon it on behalf of this group. According to the explanatory notes, the purpose of this bill is to make provision for representation in the Senate of the territories which form part of the Dominion of Canada which are not included in any province, as authorized by the act of 1886.
I fully appreciate and well understand the interest of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) in this subject, and his desire to see the Yukon and the territories have representation in the upper house or, shall I say, the upper house which some say is the counterpart in the parliament of Canada of the House of Lords in Great Britain. I know he has been interested in this subject, and I presume this is a good political move with regard to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories which contain the two constituencies that have recently been created.
However, in our opinion, Mr. Speaker, this move is a bit premature. You know, the members of this group always try to make two and two make four. We want to make certain what the future holds before we move forward, to make certain that what we are doing is necessary under the circumstances and will be of genuine advantage to the people concerned, not just of advantage to one individual. We say the bill is premature because, in our opinion, these areas should first become provinces and have selfgovernment like the other provinces that are represented in the upper house of this parliament. That definition should please its members. We should proceed in these matters a step at a time. First of all, let us provide

for self-government in the areas by virtue of the establishment of provinces. It is obvious that to date no government of Canada has considered that the population in the territories concerned could justify a provincial government or the expenses of its administration and so on. However, that is a matter of debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member
a question?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext: If what the hon. member says is correct and we are premature, and since the territories are not yet provinces, can the hon. member suggest the reason why, as far back as 1886, the mother of parliament was far-sighted enough to include in the provisions of the British North America Act a provision for the appointment of senators from the existing provinces and from all the territories which, for the time being, do not form part of the provinces but form a part of the Dominion of Canada?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I can well understand that inclusion because the persons who drafted the legislation would interpret the legislation as the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) would on occasion, in the light of all the circumstances. In our opinion, the circumstances are such that the move on the part of the hon. member is somewhat premature for several reasons. First of all, we believe there should be a provincial government. Then, too, the question of Senate reform is in the air, or am I mistaken, Mr. Speaker? Is it up in the air? We are not quite sure what is going to happen in that respect. Before we approve of a measure such as this, I feel we should know exactly what the Prime Minister has in mind with regard to Senate reform. This is one of those unrevealed mysteries to date. We give that as a second reason, Mr. Speaker, for suggesting that, with all the good intentions in the world, this measure is somewhat premature.
Then again, the population would not justify the additional expense at this time. We believe that rather than create the additional expense, it would be more businesslike, shall I say, more practical, for additional moneys to be paid to members from the Yukon and other northern members to travel their constituency to a greater extent than is possible today. I believe that would be a more practical way. It would be far better to have members of parliament representing these northern constituencies provided with sufficient funds to go to these isolated places. We certainly understand the difficulties involved and the exceptional expenditures
British North America Act required as compared with representing a riding like Wentworth, for instance. It would be far better to have three members doing that than have a representative in the Senate and three members from these ridings simply representing the area in the House of Commons or in the upper house without sufficient funds to travel their constituencies. I suggest the cost of a senator could be used to better advantage in that way.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit another question?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member agrees with me on the fundamental principle that there should be no taxation without representation. Since the other place has, in effect, a veto on taxation measures passed in this house, does the hon. member not think the citizens of the north should have a voice in the place where they are, in effect, faced with laws which impose taxes upon them?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I think the hon. member's question is very easy to answer. In so far as the realities of taxation are concerned with respect to the people of Canada, the control exists in the House of Commons. I am quite sure that people are well protected, and I am quite sure the people of the Yukon are well represented in that respect. I am sure the hon. member for the Yukon will make certain that the people of his district are protected with regard to taxation, and they will have their views considered through him.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext: That is true; but just recently the other place, for instance, refused to pass an item affecting the customs tariff. Now, there again the other place completely nullified the action taken by this house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
This was not a case within the scope of the Department of National Revenue. It was not on the basis of a form of taxation that the bill was opposed by the gentlemen in the other place. It was opposed because it was considered something new in Canadian history, the denial of the right of appeal. The Senate were protecting the people of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
I do not wish to prevent other members from having the opportunity to speak. However, I wanted to give the house some reasons why this group considered this bill somewhat premature. We are not willing, therefore, to support a measure of this type at this time because we do not believe the appointment of a senator to the upper house representing the areas specified is justified under present circumstances.

British North America Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Before the hon. member takes his seat, I wonder if he would answer a question which arises out of his initial remarks? Does he not feel representation in the parliament of Canada, including the other place, would be of benefit to Canadians who live in the north?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I tried to make the point before that it might from a theoretical point of view be a benefit. However, their representation would be greatly increased by providing the members of parliament elected from those northern areas with the funds required to travel and meet all their constituents, rather than by spending this additional money in the appointment of a senator to the Senate of Canada to represent that area.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
should like also to take this opportunity of congratulating the obviously sincere hon. member for the Yukon upon the introduction of Bill No. C-28. I was interested in this particular bill, so this afternoon I took the opportunity to check on the latest census figures. I note that the Yukon electoral district now has 14,628 people; the Northwest Territories, 22,998 and Mackenzie, 14,895. To me this is sufficient reason why representation should be given in the Senate.
I was very interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). All of a sudden the hon. member appears to be interested in saving dollars and cents. I have with me a book entitled "The Government of Canada" written by MacGregor Dawson and I should like to quote from it as it is appropriate in an argument against the cost involved, as put forward by the hon. member. It reads:
-the Senate was intended to act as a revising and restraining body to deal with possible errors or impulses of the Commons. On this point the opinion of Sir John A. Macdonald may be taken as typical:
There would be no use of an upper house if it did not exercise, when it thought proper, the right of opposing or amending or postponing the legislation of the lower house. It would be of no value whatever were it a mere chamber for registering the decrees of the lower house. It must be an independent house, having a free action of its own, for it is only valuable as being a regulating body, calmly considering the legislation initiated by the popular branch, and preventing any hasty or ill-considered legislation which may come from that body, but it will never set itself in opposition against the deliberate and understood wishes of the people.
Apparently the hon. member for Kootenay West is a perfectionist. Therefore he makes no mistakes and can see no reason why the people of that area should have representation in the Senate. I wholeheartedly support the views of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) regarding the appointment of

an Eskimo to the Senate. The Prime Minister appointed the first Indian to the upper chamber and, as I say, again I support the views expressed by the hon. member for Yukon in this regard.
In the north we have such cities as Whitehorse and Yellowknife, that are growing daily. I have had some experience in the north and have travelled through it on two or three occasions. It is indeed a fast growing area and at the moment I wish to make reference to a speech made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Dinsdale) at Winnipeg, some six months ago. He said that a satisfactory program for the north must clearly give full weight to natural resources development. It would fail, however, if it overlooked the human resources in the 35,000 people who live there. The territories are not overcrowded yet and it is startling to think that part of the country has a smaller percentage of people living there than in some of our larger cities. The population of the north is growing faster in percentage terms than any other Canadian province. Since the 1956 census estimate there has been a 60 per cent increase in population. I do not know if this is the actual figure. It is the greatest asset for development that the territories have.
I just want to go on record once more as saying that I wholeheartedly support this measure.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I would also like to commend the hon. member for Yukon for bringing this bill before the house. Anyone who has done considerable travelling in northern Canada can see the real need for the bill.
As a representative of a far northern riding and having had the opportunity recently of making an extended tour of the north, right up to the Arctic, I have seen the rapid growth that is taking place in that area. It would do a lot of hon. members good to see the development in progress in the north, and accompanying it the increase in population.
I also want to commend the hon. member for bringing the bill before the house in order to give the franchise to the people of Keewatin and Franklin districts. Returning to the present bill I, as one who represents a large population of Indian people, can fully realize what it has meant to those people to have a representative in the upper house. I know the great task which the hon. senator who represents that vast population has to do, and I can see great possibilities in the Eskimo population having a similar representative.
I know the hon. member for Kootenay West was talking about saving money, but when

one looks at the vastness of the north country and understands that these people want better representation than what they have at present, then his argument does not bear much weight. In conclusion I would like to go on record as supporting Bill C-28.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, CONTROL OF DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: On the point of order; yesterday I said I should like to see mustard seed included. However, I said also that under the present system mustard seed cannot be included because it has no statutory definition as to grade under the Canada Grain Act. It is not listed as a statutory grade in that act, neither is it listed under the western division which we find in the act on page 60. Consequently, I think, we shall not be able to bring mustard seed under the provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. Only western grain can be brought within the provisions of that act. In the Canadian Wheat Board Act it is stated that grain includes wheat, oats, barley, rye and flax seed. It is stated further in the Canada Grain Act, in section 2, that western grain means grain grown in the western division, and the western division means all that portion of Canada lying west of the meridian passing through the eastern boundary of the city of Port Arthur. Thus I regret very much that we cannot include mustard seed at the present time because it would be out of order to do so. I suggest that the amendment cannot comply with the regulations set out in the Canada Grain Act and in the Canadian Wheat Board Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, CONTROL OF DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
On the point of order, all I can say is that the remarks we have just heard come strangely from a member who obviously, on the basis of his past efforts, is interested in having these regulations apply to mustard seed. It is strange he should argue that the amendment is out of order.
However, I would remind the Chair that we are dealing now with the Canadian Wheat Board Act and that the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale, in arguing that this amendment is out of order, has referred to another act altogether. The definition of grain in the Canadian Wheat Board Act does not depend, according to that act, on some other legislation. It stands on its own feet. I submit that if this phrase "and mustard seed" were added it would be within the

Canadian Wheat Board Act jurisdiction of the wheat board to decide whether or not quota regulations would apply to mustard seed. It might well be that action should be taken to define grades of mustard seed under the Canada Grain Act, but I suggest that is another proposition and that it has to do with another act. In my view it is very much in order to amend the act which we are now considering by adding the words "and mustard seed" in addition to the amendment which is already before the Chair, namely that which refers to rapeseed. For these reasons I suggest we should deal with this matter not by declaring it out of order but by putting the amendment before the committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, CONTROL OF DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Further to the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct your attention to chapter 25 of the Canada Grain Act, where it refers to statutory grades of western grain. Perhaps I might read the grains which appear in the western schedule. They are: red spring wheat, winter wheat, amber Durum, mixed wheat, oats, barley, rye, mixed grain, flax seed, buckwheat, corn, sunflower seed, soybeans, peas and rapeseed. Your Honour will find that these are the grains which come under the western schedule. Only those grains come under the Canadian wheat board which are listed in the western grain schedule.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, CONTROL OF DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a word about the point of order. It seems to me that the point of order almost is answered by the fact that the whole purpose of the clause we have before us is precisely to amend the present list of grains to include rapeseed, and if it is competent for the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre to introduce an amendment to include rape-seed surely it is equally competent for the hon. member for Assiniboia to introduce an amendment to include mustard seed. Order. I feel I have had enough assistance from hon. members of the committee at this stage and wish to thank


them for the help they have given. I do not reject an amendment on the basis of whether or not it would be better put to a vote in the committee to let the committee decide, because I would fear the bad practice of establishing a precedent by which the Chair or his successors may not be able to abide. I start with the premise that is set out in section 59, paragraph 2 of the standing orders which reads as follows:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
That standing order is well known to all hon. members of the committee. If I may, I should like to refer to May's sixteenth edition at page 421 the opening paragraph under the heading "Rules with Respect to the form and Content of Amendments" which reads as follows:
The fundamental rule that debate must be relevant to a question necessarily involves the rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed-
It goes on to say:
Stated generally, no matter ought to be raised in debate on a question which would be irrelevant, if moved as an amendment, and an amendment cannot be used for importing arguments which would be irrelevant to the main question.
Paragraph 1 on page 554 dealing with the topic "Amendments" reads as follows:
An amendment is out of order if it is irrelevant to the subject matter or beyond the scope of the bill, or if it is irrelevant to the subject matter or beyond the scope of the clause under consideration.
This is the authority which leads me to believe that the committee should weigh very carefully the complex question of introducing a word which might enlarge the scope of the clause under consideration.
Finally, may I refer to the explanatory notes of the bill itself which generally describe the purpose of the bill. The explanatory note to clause 1 reads as follows:
The purpose of the amendment to paragraph (e) is to redefine grain to include rapeseed.
This is cast in pretty ironclad terms. It is for this reason that I feel the addition of the words "mustard seed" in the clause under consideration would enlarge the scope of the bill. I see that the hon. member for Ottawa West is anxious to rise to his feet. If he has something further to offer to assist the Chair I would be very glad to hear him.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, CONTROL OF DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word if I may about the point of order. The explanatory notes have no relevance at all in consideration of the matter because they can have no effect before the committee. If a minister includes explanatory notes in a bill that do not accurately explain

what is being done by the bill, that surely cannot restrict the bill when it is before the house or the committee for consideration. It is the bill itself at which we must look in order to determine the question of relevance or whether or not the proposed amendment is foreign to the object of the bill itself. That must remain the test.
On the question of whether or not the proposition embodied in the amendment offered is relevant, I should like if I may to point out exactly what the part of the clause with which we are concerned says. It is an amendment to the definition of the word "grain" which in the act reads " 'grain' includes wheat, oats, barley, rye and flaxseed" and the amendment merely adds the words "and rapeseed". In other words the word "grain" is being enlarged in part by adding another of the oil seeds to the definition.
The word "grain" it will be seen does not contain an inclusive definition but is defined by listing certain cereal grains and certain oil seeds. That is the method the government used in approaching the definition of the word. The amendment offered is merely to enlarge the number of oil seeds being included in that definition, so it is not foreign to the clause in the bill before us. It is squarely within it. It is adding after the definition now included in the bill the words "and mustard seed", which is another one of the oil seeds. Surely it would be perfectly competent, for instance, Mr. Chairman, to suggest that the word "grain" should include all the cereal grains and the oil seeds. It would be quite impractical to do it as a proposition for the house to adopt but surely it would be perfectly competent to redefine the word "grain" by offering an amendment that said simply that it includes all cereal grains and all oil seeds.
Since the bill is put forward in the form that it designates certain cereal grains and certain oil seeds, what is being offered here is an addition to the oil seeds already included in the definition. Surely that is competent. For instance, it would be competent to offer an amendment that would limit rapeseed to certain grades of rapeseed as defined under the Canada Grain Act, or to restrict them in any way. Here we are merely extending the definition of the oil seeds to include mustard seed.

I should like to quote from an article in La Terre de Chez Nous which appeared in the issue of November 29, 1961. It is an article which deals with this question of feed grains and with what happened when the government decided last fall to authorize the feed companies to import quantities of grain, particularly feed oats, from the United States. It reads:
[The Chairman.]
Feed is not "for the asking"; it must be paid for and at a high price just now. This is a common complaint. It is heard throughout eastern Canada-from the head of the Great Lakes to the easternmost tip of Newfoundland. In Quebec and Ontario, the various mixtures are selling from $1 to $5 or $6 a ton more than a year ago, and in some cases the difference is even much greater.
As everyone knows, the cause of the trouble is the small quantity of grains used in making feed, particularly oats and barley. Another well-known fact is that when stocks are limited, prices climb quickly especially at the consumer level. In the case of feed grains, the leading consumer, the one who foots most of the bill, is the eastern farmer. His plight is the greater because of the fact that products obtained from these grains show no sky-rocketing tendencies.
However, it must be admitted that the prices of oats and barley are no longer at the top of the ladder as they were in August. They have dropped a little, maybe two or three rungs, according to official quotations. The entry into Canada of a few million bushels of oats from the United States has had a wholesome effect; that fact must be recognized. According to one of our best economists, these American imports have helped reduce by about $3 to $4 a ton the price of oats and barley in Canada.
That quotation is taken from a newspaper published in the hon. member's own province. I might say in this connection that from August 17 to February 16, 1962, the board has issued permits for the importation of 10,370,300 bushels of United States oats. Each permit had a 30 day expiry limit and not all of the permits were exercised. Over 5,200,000 bushels of American oats have been brought into Canada, mostly to eastern Canadian positions, half of which have been used up and the remainder is still in storage.
At March 1 this year there were over 6 million bushels of feed oats in the elevators in eastern Canada. This included about
2.400.000	bushels of American oats and a small quantity of eastern Canadian oats. This total is almost double the quantity of oats in eastern positions at March 1 last year, when only
3.400.000	bushels were on hand.
Supply of Canadian feed oats in store at the lakehead at March 1 this year amounted to 7,300,000 bushels compared with only
3.400.000	bushels at March 1, 1961. Therefore the hon. member's charge that the Canadian wheat board has not been recognizing the difficulties of the eastern feeders is not well founded, and the charge that the board has done nothing to assist the eastern feeders is one which cannot be substantiated, as is shown by the article I quoted from La Terre de Chez Nous and as is indicated by the statement I have just made.
I am sure that the hon. member, on reflection, would be prepared to say that the Canadian wheat board has made a very strenuous effort to ensure that quantities of feed have been made available to eastern feeders at all times.

I would like some information from either the minister or the parliamentary secretary on what is really involved in this clause. Its scope is obvious. It states:
With the approval of the governor in council, the board may enter into a contract with any person
(a)	for the provision of a group life insurance plan, and
(b)	for the provision of a group medical-surgical insurance plan
for the members of the board and the officers, clerks and employees employed by the board under this act and their dependants, and may contribute a share of the premiums payable under such plans out of the funds of the board.
Subclause (2) reads:
Contributions made by the board pursuant to subsection (1) shall be deemed to be expenses incurred in connection with the operations of the board.
It is perfectly clear what this will allow to be done. With the approval of the governor in council contracts can be entered into to provide group life insurance and group medical-surgical insurance for members, officers and clerks of the board, and the farmers will foot the bill. The farmers will pay the cost out of the wheat board funds.
Now I am not objecting to this. I want to make that clear; but I believe the minister owes it to the committee to tell us how many employees could be covered by this clause, and give us some idea of the thinking that went into bringing this important amendment before the house. Has the wheat board on hand some tentative proposals with regard to this kind of coverage? If so, what would the cost be, and how many employees are involved. I think the grain producers of western Canada who are going to have to 26207-1-143
Canadian Wheat Board Act foot the bill and pay these costs, or a portion of them, have the right to know what may be involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, CONTROL OF DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: The thinking behind this amendment, of course, is obvious. It is consideration for the employees of a first class business organization. It is just good business practice, recognized also in government circles, to provide the type of benefit which the board would like to provide for its employees in this amendment. I am sure the producers of western Canada who are now paying the salaries of the Canadian wheat board and the employees of that board would be only too pleased to go this step further, as most business enterprises are doing today, and provide for group life insurance and group medical-surgical insurance for the employees of the board. This is a contributory plan. It is not simply a handout on the part of the producers. However, there is the normal share paid by the employer toward the cost of the plans. What that means in dollars and cents I cannot say immediately because I have not got the figures in front of me showing the number of employees but, of course, that is readily available. I would think that after approval has been given to this measure, when the officials of the wheat board are here, as they are before the committee on agriculture every year, the detailed questions which the hon. member for Assiniboia has raised could very well be answered. However, unless hon. members intend to oppose this forward step I am not certain that we need go into some of the details the hon. member has mentioned.

I was trying to find out whether there have been any discussions with the board concerning any binding agreements or contracts which could be entered into with the employees with the approval of the governor in council to provide for group life insurance and group medical-surgical insurance. The minister says this information is readily available. This information is not readily available. The minister comes into this house without the figures for which I have been asking. I am not saying he should carry them all in his mind or even

in his briefcase. But I say that he should have the officials before this committee so that we can obtain this information. I say, Mr. Chairman, that in all my time in parliament I have never known a minister of the crown say to me in response to a question I put to him: "Oh, sit down". I think that is the height of arrogance from an arrogant minister in an arrogant government. It is hardly fitting coming from a minister in a government which says it does not want to impose closure but wants parliament to have the right to free discussion.
The grain producers of western Canada are being asked in this clause to give the government the right to impose an additional burden on grain producers. I am not saying they will object to the contracts. I think the grain producers have shown that they want an efficient wheat board efficiently run. But I also believe that in a time of crop failure and low incomes to grain producers, at a time when the government has felt, with the support of all the members of the house, that steps should be taken to do at least something to alleviate this situation, it is pertinent to ask how much this is going to cost-how much it may cost. I have the greatest regard for the personnel of the Canadian wheat board but I make the statement that people who are receiving salaries of $20,000 a year or more are just a little more capable of providing their own life insurance and their own group medical-surgical insurance than the hard-pressed grain producers who will be asked to foot the bill.
I do not intend to oppose the clause. I am going to vote for it. If the minister wants to call a vote, I shall vote for it; but I think it is a very bad thing for the minister to come here and ask parliament to rubberstamp this proposal, though it be the best clause in the world, without giving us the kind of information for which I have asked. While I shall vote for it, I wager that there are tens of thousands of grain producers who would say that in view of the attitude of the government it is an imposition in a year of crop failure to ask them for this kind of blank cheque without any explanation. It is not enough to say to parliament, "Pass it tonight and we will give you the information at some later date when we have a meeting of the agriculture committee".
