There is one point I should like to have clarified with regard to clause 2. The difficulty in which I find myself arises out of the fact that the explanatory note says something quite different from what is contained in the clause itself. The clause provides that the board may, with the approval of the governor in council, work out a group life insurance plan or a group medical surgical plan. From that provision I take it that it is quite clear that what is envisaged is an attempt to bring the provision for the employees in line with the provisions usually made for employees in the government service and in larger private corporations, where there are sufficient numbers of them to work out a scheme of this kind. That is what is intended here, I take it. However, what I am not clear about is the latter part of subclause (1) of the new clause 8A wherein it is provided that "the board may contribute a share of the premiums payable under such plans out of the funds of the board". The explanatory notes say something quite different from that latter part of the clause which I have quoted. The explanatory notes say that the board would be permitted to contribute the employers' share of the cost. There is no such limitation on the board at all. The board could contribute much more than the employers' share. In the proposed legislation there is no limitation on them. What I want to know from the minister is this. Does he envisage any part of what is usually called the employers' share in these joint schemes being provided by the government and not by the board itself through the producers? The act is wide open in its language and permits payment from any source. It is merely permissive with the board to pay a part of the share if it so wishes. Does he envisage that

any part of the employers' share will be paid by the federal government out of public funds?

I should like to ask a question on clause 4 merely in order to get the opinion of the minister and the government. Some farm organizations-and I refer particularly to the national farmers union-have been asking that the Canadian Wheat Board Act be made a permanent one. I am not positive in my own mind just how that would be done if it were the intention of the government to do so, but I take it you would merely omit the termination date for these various pool periods and omit any termination date anywhere in the act.
I can see arguments both ways. I think what the producers have in mind is this. They want to be reassured that the Canadian Wheat Board Act is in fact a permanent statute and that there is no intention to bring it to an end. On the other hand, there is the argument on the other side that parliament every once in a while-by this amendment it would be five years from now-should have the chance to review the act. I can see good arguments on both sides. I am simply wondering whether the government has considered the representations of the national farmers union and what the thinking of the government is in making the termination date August 1, 1967.
I have no doubt that a future parliament prior to that date will extend the act for a further period. I cannot conceive of any government likely to be elected in this country throwing out the Canadian Wheat Board Act. Nevertheless the farmers in this country wish to be reassured that for all practical purposes this is permanent legislation.

I think the hon. member for Assiniboia is quite right, that no future parliament would destroy the wheat board. Nevertheless, in conversation with the Minister of Agriculture we reached the conclusion that there might be some advantage in bringing forward for review at five year periods the operations of the wheat board.
As a matter of fact, I read the debate that occurred five years ago on this subject and may I say that the hon. member for Assiniboia made a very good speech on that occasion. It was well thought out and, insofar as Hansard indicates, moderately delivered. There were no interruptions.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, CONTROL OF DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, clause 5 has to do with changing some words with regard to defining the separate account. I have read the clause carefully and it may clarify the provision for a separate account so-called in certain circumstances. I can see nothing of a substantive change in this clause.
However, at this time I do wish to get from the minister, if I can, information as to the amount of money in the separate account and the amount of money, if any, that has been paid out of the separate account during the last few years. In particular I should like to refer to one very large payment which, according to the annual report of the Canadian wheat board for the crop year 1959-60, was paid out of the separate account by authority of order in council P.C. 1960-519. The report contains this statement:
On September 23, 1959, the out-shore annex of the United Grain Growers Limited terminal elevator "A" at Port Arthur, Ontario, collapsed. The collapse resulted in the loss of 1,194,760.1 bushels of wheat, oats and barley valued at $2,406,175.22.
From this information I take it that the United Grain Growers came to the government and said, "Look, we have had an accident. We have lost over $2,406,000. Will you help us out by taking $775,000 from the special account and making us this gift?" I am just saying that is my interpretation. If I am wrong, I ask the minister to correct me.
As I understand the situation, this special account originates from the fact that over the years, with so many grain producers accounts, some payments are not claimed; and with such huge sums of money involved in total over the years the moneys unclaimed have accumulated to a sizeable amount. I am prepared to listen to arguments and to say that I could be persuaded I am wrong, but my impression at this time is that this is not the best use to be made of these funds.
The minister can claim, and rightly so, that the United Grain Growers Limited is a farm organization and that this is a case of taking funds out of the special account in the general wheat board fund and paying the

money to a farmers' grain organization. I would also think that if a private grain company suffered the same kind of disaster it would have an equal claim, and I think it should have an equal claim for payment out of this fund. But if you are going to take funds out of a special account and pay them to grain companies I think that in itself is not the best use to be made of those funds.
I remember that when this legislation was first proposed years ago I said I would far rather see this money in the separate account paid into the general wheat board funds and go into the pockets of the grain producers in total. I suppose the only argument against that is that in relation to the total number of grain producers there is not so much money involved per grain producer and that it would be better to use the money in a chunk to greater advantage than to divide it among all producers. That is the argument on the other side perhaps, but I do not think it is valid in this case because the money has been paid to a group of grain producers instead of to all grain producers. I think this is a bad precedent and I hope it will not be followed in the future.
I want to say that I think that many of the uses to which this money has been put are excellent. Bringing over trade missions that may buy larger quantities of grain and using the money generally for the promotion of markets for all grain producers are good ways to use the money, but 1 do question the wisdom of making a handout, which is all it was in my opinion, to an elevator company even when that elevator company has suffered a disaster. I think this is not the right way to use the funds in this account.
I do not have the information that is available to the minister at my fingertips and I am prepared to be persuaded I am wrong. It may be because I lack some of the information that I have come to this conclusion, but I should like to hear from the minister what particular events or arguments persuaded the governor in council to take $775,000 out of this special account of the Canadian wheat board and pay it to the United Grain Growers.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, CONTROL OF DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this was one of the most difficult problems that faced me as minister with some responsibility for the wheat board in the year 1959 and the spring of 1960. It involved a great many meetings and consultations between ministers of the government and representatives of the United Grain Growers, a tremendous amount of work on the part of the law officers of the crown consulting with representatives from the
Canadian Wheat Board Act United Grain Growers. The situation is now, of course, two years old. The settlement was reached two years ago.
However, the hon. member's query is a fair one. Should the money in the special fund be used for a purpose such as this? I tell you quite frankly that that was the question which was considered time and time again in the course of the many meetings that were held with regard to this problem. The problem arose as a result of the collapse of an elevator at the lakehead, one of the unforeseen hazards with regard to elevators. If my memory serves me correctly, at the time I asked if anyone could tell me of any similar occurrence in Canadian history. Relying again on my memory, I think they said no, other than the collapse of a wooden elevator that had grown very old. However, this was an elevator situation on the shore of the lake; the foundation gave way and the elevator collapsed. We are very fortunate that there was no loss of life because a ship was scheduled to arrive at the wharf for loading within a few hours of the collapse. Had the ship been tied up beside the wharf, the ship might have been destroyed, in addition to the elevator, and there may have been loss of life as well.
Well, we were faced with this situation, that there might have been litigation, a suit against the wheat board. The amount of money involved would have been tied up pending a settlement by the court, and that would have affected the final payment in the spring of 1960 for the earlier crop year. We had to consider this situation, that 50,000 producers, members of the United Grain Growers organization, would have to bear the entire cost and might therefore be embarrassed financially. A decision was reached to draw from the special fund, largely on these grounds: That the disaster which occurred only in one elevator and to one elevator company was unprecedented and unlikely to occur in the future; that it was something against which adequate insurance provision could not be made. In addition, we thought it was unwise to tie up the final payment by paying money into court until a settlement was reached. Then, too, we thought that spreading this unprecedented loss over a very large field by drawing upon the special fund might be the best way out of the difficulty.
Whether the decision was right or wrong, time alone will tell. I do not doubt but that it could be criticized on some ground. Perhaps other people would have made a different decision. We ended up by reaching what appeared to us to be a reasonable settlement and came to the assistance of 50,000 wheat producers who own their own elevator system, and placed no penalty on any producer in the country, because the special fund was of

Canadian Wheat Board Act such a size at that time that it was possible to draw upon it in that amount without interfering with the other uses to which the fund is put from time to time. I suggest that is the background of that particular incident, and our hope is that no such disaster will aifect any of the elevator companies in the future or any of the producer organizations.

speechtext:
I appreciate the answer the minister has given. I cannot express an opinion tonight on the legal questions involved. I have no idea, myself, as to the grounds upon which the United Grain Growers would press any claim for damages against the Canadian wheat board. However, I do think that the government should be most careful in using this fund for this kind of purpose. I do not see, myself, how this situation could have any real bearing on the final payment because the amount involved, a million dollars or so, just could not tie up the whole of the final payment which would be a much larger sum of money than that.
I can see how it might tie up $2.4 million, but even then I think the wheat board could borrow the money within about 60 minutes if that were necessary, because the wheat board is handling huge sums of money and has assets probably hundreds of times greater than the $2.4 million involved.
I have a natural inclination to think of the individual grain producer. It is for this reason I have been putting forward these remarks tonight and stating the position of the grain growers as a whole as opposed to action which provided assistance for 50,000 grain growers out of almost 250,000. If the individual farmer who has to take his grain to the wheat board suffers a disaster on his farm, he foots the bill. The individual farmer has no recourse to anyone of whom I am aware. However, it is interesting to note that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in an appendix to its brief this year, set forth a policy asking for emergency loan legislation for individual farmers suffering a disaster.
I will read the first paragraph of this submission:
Occasionally farming areas are struck by sudden natural catastrophes such as severe drought, large scale floods, storms of hurricane force, severe infestations of insects, plant diseases of epidemic proportions, severe frosts at certain periods for plant and tree growth and other natural hazards.


This is a new aspect of farm policy requesting extraordinary action in time of disaster to the individual farmer. Perhaps this scheme would be a difficult thing for the wheat board to administer. It would perhaps be difficult to make any of these moneys available to an individual farmer who suffers a disaster, but I put it to the minister that if a farmer loses one year's crop, this is a much greater disaster from his point of view than the disaster affecting an individual even though he be a shareholder in the United Grain Growers. Perhaps this could be made something of a revolving fund out of which moneys could be made available to help individual producers who face individual disasters.
The minister has given us an explanation of the long discussions that took place in making these moneys available. I shall not accuse him tonight of having made a wrong decision but I believe that in his own mind he certainly thought this was a borderline case. However, if errors are to be made I would prefer to see errors of judgment made on the side of helping the individual producer and not helping to bail out a grain company from a disaster, even though that grain company may be owned by producers. If it is United Grain Growers today it could be some other company tomorrow, and this fund could be used in a way which parliament never intended when the legislation passed through this house.
